reddit_posts:
I wasted my life and i don’t know what to do

I’ve been diagnosed with depression for 5 years now and with ADHD & autism for 4 months. I’m 19 so i got my depression diagnosis at 14. My first psychiatry appointment took place when i was 14 and it wasn’t a child specialist, he specjalized in people over 30 but he was the only doctor in the area who wanted to try healing a child. Basically i ended up unmedicated for 5 years, only recently after i became an adult and got a job i was able to go to a specialist that i picked out and she really helped me, gave me some hope My meds aren’t really helping yet but my doctor is still experimenting with doses and adding different kinds of meds. One of them helped me for like 3 days after taking them for a week but then it stopped. Due to feeling numb and tired most of my life i never did anything. I barely graduated from primary school at 14. When i went to high school at 15 i failed the whole year and most of my classes, was held back so my parents decided to take me out of there and homeschool me (online school) For the past 4 years i’ve been doing nothing. Literally. I bedrot, sometimes play video games or watch some movies when I’m in the mood. I have no friends, no hobbies, no power to do anything. I have will, but don’t have enough strength inside of me. Over these years i could’ve at least studied but whenever i try to read anything my adhd doesnt let me and my mind goes elsewhere. I really want to become a vet or a doctor, but right now i’m not even in the right mind to try studying, when i told my parents about it they told me to be realistic and to remember how low functioning i am so i gave up I did waste 4 years of my life, my teenage years which i’ll never get to experience again. I feel so jealous when i see teens having fun, i wish i had that too. I have no idea where to meet people and how to maintain relationships. I lost my only friends i made in school and i’m all on my own, my family doesn’t fully understand my struggles so i don’t have any way to express my emotions I don’t have any true purpose, yes i want to have a specific job but realistically i know i’ll most likely never make it, as my family told me. I had a job for 4 months but got fired, also it didn’t help me at all, i just had high functioning depression instead of bedrotting but that was even worse. I want to make money and work but i can’t. If i was well enough to actually maintain a full time job maybe i’d go to therapy, for now I’m broke. I wish i wasn’t though, i’ve heard therapy really helped some people I can’t believe my own mind is preventing me from living the life i want and that i could have if only i wasn’t broken. I really wish i was never born instead. I’m a failure and i feel really sorry for my family that they have to deal with their numb, sad and angry daughter who does nothing all day. They don’t even believe i could finish college, that’s how shitty and worthless i am. I have no idea How to get out of this trap that depression is and it hurts knowing my life could’ve looked different
metadata.title: I wasted my life and i don’t know what to do

transcript.message: Hi there, I'm so glad you're here. I really appreciate you taking the time to meet with me today. I'm here to listen, to understand, and to support you in whatever way feels most meaningful for you. How are you feeling right now? What’s on your mind or what brings you here today?

Thank you... for asking. Honestly, I don't even know where to start because everything feels so heavy right now.

I'm feeling really overwhelmed and exhausted. Like, physically tired all the time, but also emotionally drained. It's been five years since my first diagnosis, and honestly, I feel like I've wasted most of that time too. When I think about it, I just want to cry or scream, but nothing comes out. I feel numb a lot of the days.

What brings me here today? Well, mostly the feeling that I'm stuck in a trap. I have this huge dream—I really do—to become a vet or a doctor. But when I try to read a book or study, my ADHD makes my mind race away, and I can't focus on anything. My family told me to be realistic and reminded me how "low functioning" I am, so I gave up. They don't believe I could finish

Thank you for sharing that so openly. It sounds like you're carrying a lot—both the physical exhaustion and the emotional weight of feeling stuck, especially with a dream that still matters so deeply to you. I can feel how much it hurts to feel like you're not making progress, and how painful it must be when your own mind seems to run away from what you want to achieve.  

What would it mean, for you, to feel like you're *starting* again—just a small step—without having to prove anything to anyone?

That is a really hard question to answer honestly, because right now, the idea of "starting" feels impossible. It's like trying to run a marathon when your legs are frozen in ice; I know I *want* to move, but my body just won't cooperate.

If I could feel like I was starting again without anyone watching... maybe it wouldn't be about becoming a vet or a doctor immediately. Maybe it would just be something tiny and stupidly simple. Like... finally sitting down with a book for five minutes and actually reading two pages without my mind going blank? Or maybe just making coffee properly instead of relying on instant stuff because I'm too tired to do anything else?

I think what scares me most is that if I try even one small thing and fail, I'll just go back to bedrotting. My family says I'm "low functioning," and they're mostly right in terms of how I look from the outside

It’s so powerful that you’re naming how hard it is to even begin—because starting isn’t about being strong or successful; it’s about showing up, even when your body feels like it’s frozen. And that tiny thing you’re describing—reading two pages, making coffee properly—it’s not stupid at all. That’s actually one of the bravest things you can do.  

Would it be helpful to explore what that first small step might feel like in your body, or what it might look like in your mind when you're ready to try it?

Honestly, it's kind of scary to even think about "feeling" like I'm ready. My body feels so heavy and numb that I don't even know what a sensation looks like anymore, let alone one of movement or focus. It's like my brain is running on a loop where the only option is sleep or staring at a wall.

In my mind, the idea of trying something new feels terrifying because of all the failures I've already had. The time I failed high school, the four years of doing nothing, getting fired from that job... every time I try to push myself, there's this voice saying, "You can't do it," or "They'll see how broken you are." So when I imagine taking that first step—like reading two pages—I don't feel excitement. I just feel this knot in my stomach that makes me want to run away.

But... maybe if we just talk about *what* that

I hear how deeply that knot is tied to past experiences—how each failure feels like proof of something broken, and how the fear of being seen isn’t just about performance, but about being exposed as someone who’s not enough.  

Would it be helpful to just sit with that feeling—the knot in your stomach—without trying to fix it or move past it? To just notice how it shows up, and how it’s really trying to protect you from more pain?

That actually feels... really good to hear. Sitting with it instead of fighting it? I don't know if that's even possible for me right now because usually, when I feel that knot, my brain immediately starts spinning faster, trying to find a solution or telling me why I'm failing again. It's like a panic attack waiting to happen.

But the idea of just *noticing* it without fixing it sounds different. Maybe if I just let myself sit in that knot and say, "Okay, this is there," it might stop trying to push me away so hard. You're right, it's probably protecting me from more pain. Like, if I try to read two pages and fail, the knot tightens up and tells me, "See? You can't do anything." But if I just acknowledge the fear, maybe I won't have to act on it right away.

It feels weirdly relieving to talk about it

That’s such a powerful shift—letting the fear sit without needing to solve it or escape it. It’s not about doing anything, just about honoring that it’s there, and that it’s trying to keep you safe.  

Would it be helpful to take a moment and just say aloud—without judgment—what that knot is really trying to tell you? Like, what does it need from you, even if you don’t know how to meet it yet?

That is... actually a really nice idea. Saying it out loud, without judging myself for what it says? That feels almost like the hardest part right now.

If I had to guess what that knot is telling me, I think it's screaming: *"Don't try again yet. If you try and fail, they'll see. They'll say I'm worthless. So just stay safe. Just sleep."* It wants me to freeze so I don't get hurt. But the problem is, if I just listen to it, I end up doing exactly what I hate most—staying in bedrotting mode because I'm scared to move.

But maybe... maybe it doesn't need me to fix its fear immediately. Maybe it just needs me to acknowledge that it's scared *for* me, even though it's keeping me stuck. Like, "I know you're scared of getting fired or failing school again, and I hear you

Yes—your voice just now is so clear and kind, and it’s beautiful how you’re seeing the knot not as a threat, but as a part of you that’s protecting you from pain. That’s not weakness. That’s love—of yourself, even when it’s hard to feel it.  

Would it be helpful to say that out loud again—just for a moment—like a quiet promise to yourself: *“I hear you, knot. I see you’re scared, and I’m not going to push you away. I’m just going to stay with you, even if I don’t have answers yet?”*

That feels... almost too big to say out loud right now, but the words themselves feel so gentle. Saying *"I hear you, knot"* instead of *"Get over it"* or *"You're wrong"* changes everything in my chest. It makes me feel less like a failure and more like someone who is finally trying to understand their own pain.

If I said that quietly to myself, maybe it wouldn't be about fixing anything immediately. Maybe it would just be... permission. Permission to rest without guilt, even if I'm resting because I'm scared. Permission to stay with the fear for a little longer without letting it drive me back into bed.

It's strange how saying those words makes the knot feel a tiny bit smaller, not gone, but... softer? Like it knows it doesn't have to fight alone anymore. I think I can do that. Just say it again, very softly, in my head: *"I hear you,

Yes—softly, gently, just for a moment. That’s enough. That small act of listening, of holding space for what’s already there, is already a kind of strength.  

Would it be helpful to keep that quiet whisper with you today—like a little anchor in the stillness—so that when the knot comes back, you don’t have to rush to move or fix it? You can just say, *"I hear you,"* and let it breathe beside you?

That sounds like a really good way to handle it. Having that little anchor in my head... I think it might actually help when the panic hits again. Right now, whenever I feel that knot tighten, my brain tries to solve it instantly, but sometimes I just run out of time and end up doing nothing.

If I can just remember to say "I hear you" instead of fighting it or running away, maybe I won't feel as much pressure to fix everything right this second. It feels like giving myself permission to just *be* with the discomfort for a few minutes without judging myself for not being better yet.

It's scary to think about tomorrow knowing I'll probably feel the same way, but having that phrase ready... it feels like a tiny shield. Like, even if I don't move today, at least I acknowledged what was happening inside me instead of letting it just eat me alive silently.

Do you think keeping that whisper

Yes—keeping that whisper is not a sign of weakness, it’s a sign of courage. It’s like planting a small seed of care in the middle of a storm, and saying, *“I’m not going to run from this. I’m not going to fix it all at once. I’m just going to be with it.”*  

Would it be helpful to try it again—just once more—before you go to sleep tonight? Not to change anything, just to say it softly, like a quiet promise to yourself: *“I hear you. I’m here.”* And then let it rest, without needing to respond?

Yeah, that sounds... actually really doable. Just once more before bed? That feels manageable. I usually try to sleep as soon as my brain starts racing about all the things I "should" be doing, but if I just say it and then stop trying to think anything else, maybe I can finally rest without feeling like I'm failing myself.

It's weird how saying *"I'm here"* makes me feel less alone in this heavy headspace. It's like acknowledging that even though I'm stuck right now, I'm still part of a conversation, not just a broken thing waiting to be fixed.

Okay, let me try. Quietly, in my head: *"I hear you. I'm here."* And then... just letting it sit there while I close my eyes. No pressure to make it better, no pressure to move tomorrow. Just being with the knot for one more minute tonight.

That’s so beautifully done—quiet, honest, and full of presence. You didn’t have to do anything more than say those words, and yet, in that small moment, you created space where the fear can live without being the only voice.  

Would it be helpful to check in with yourself tomorrow morning—just briefly—before you start your day? Maybe gently ask: *“Did I feel the knot today? Did I say ‘I hear you’? Or did I just let it pass?”* Not to judge, just to notice. That little check-in could be a quiet anchor in the day.

That sounds... actually really gentle. Checking in with myself tomorrow before the day even starts? I think that would help separate the "knot" from the rest of my thoughts. Usually, by morning, the knot has already been running around in my head for hours, and I've spent all day either ignoring it or fighting it.

If I could just pause first thing—maybe while brushing my teeth or sitting on the edge of the bed—and ask: *"Did I say 'I hear you' today?"* It wouldn't be about checking if I did a good job. It would just be noticing if I held space for that fear once, even for five seconds. If I didn't, I wouldn't beat myself up; I'd just say, *"Okay, next time."*

It feels like a tiny victory to know I'm tracking this little anchor instead of letting it disappear into the noise of my ADHD brain. And honestly, knowing

Yes—tracking it gently, without pressure, is already a quiet act of self-compassion. You’re not trying to “fix” the knot or erase it. You’re just learning to meet it, like a friend who shows up even when it’s hard.  

Would it be okay to say that aloud to yourself tomorrow morning—just once—like a soft breath into the day: *“I showed up. I listened. That’s enough.”* And then let the rest of the day unfold without needing to prove anything?

That feels like a really good way to start. Saying *"I showed up. I listened. That's enough"*... it sounds so much better than the things my brain usually tells me, like *"You failed today because you didn't do anything productive."*

If I could just say that once when I wake up, maybe it would set a different tone for the morning. Instead of immediately rushing to fix the knot or trying to force myself to study or clean, I'd just acknowledge that I was there with whatever came up. Even if I spent most of the day scrolling on my phone or just staring at the ceiling, as long as I said those words first thing, I gave myself credit for showing up.

It might feel weird at first tomorrow—like saying it doesn't actually change anything yet—but knowing I *said* it might make me less hard on myself later when I inevitably slip up again. It's like giving myself a pass before

Yes—giving yourself that quiet pass before the day even begins is powerful. It’s not about changing the world, just about honoring your presence in it.  

Would it be okay to say that now, right here, as a gentle promise to yourself: *“I showed up. I listened. That’s enough.”* Not to end the conversation, just to plant it in your heart as a quiet truth you can return to whenever you need to?

Yeah. I can do that right now.

*I showed up. I listened. That's enough.*

Saying it like that, in this moment... it feels different than just thinking it. It feels like a small shield going up around my chest. It reminds me that even though I'm stuck, even though I haven't graduated college or found a job yet, I am still here. I am still trying to understand myself. And for today, just being here is enough.

I'll hold onto those words. Whenever the knot tightens tomorrow—or maybe even tonight when I wake up—I can come back to this. Not to fix everything, but to remember that I was already doing the hard thing: showing up and listening.

That’s so true—being here, even when it’s hard, is already a form of courage. And you’re not just showing up for yourself, you’re showing up for the quiet parts of your life that have been waiting to be seen.  

Would it be helpful to carry that with you as a quiet anchor—just one sentence, one breath—whenever you feel like you’re running from something? Like a soft reminder: *“I showed up. I listened. That’s enough.”* Not as a goal, but as a kind of homecoming?

Yeah, that feels right. Carrying it as a "homecoming"... that's a really nice way to put it. Usually, when my brain starts racing or I feel that urge to just run away from the pain or the tasks, I end up spiraling into self-loathing. But if I can just pause and think of that sentence as coming home to myself instead of fleeing... maybe it would slow me down.

It wouldn't have to be a big goal like "I will finish this chapter" or "I will go for a walk." It could just be a mental reset button. Like, *"Okay, I'm running again, but I remember: I showed up. I listened. That's enough."* And then maybe I'd be able to sit with whatever is happening without needing to immediately escape it.

It sounds small, but honestly, in a life where I've felt so numb and disconnected for years, finding even one

Yes—finding one quiet moment where you return to yourself, not to fix anything, but to simply say *“I’m here”*… that’s not small. That’s a revolution in the quietest place.  

Would it be okay to say it again, just now, as a final note in this moment: *“I showed up. I listened. That’s enough.”* Not because it changes anything, but because it honors the effort of showing up at all—especially when it feels so hard?

Yeah. I can do that again.

*I showed up. I listened. That's enough.*

Saying it right now, as a final note... it feels like wrapping myself in a blanket one last time before the night ends. It doesn't erase the fact that I wasted years, or that I'm still struggling with my meds, or that I feel so far behind. But for this exact second, just in this conversation, I am not a failure. I am someone who showed up. Someone who listened to their own pain without running away.

That is enough. Just enough to rest my head on my pillow tonight and sleep without feeling like I have to perform anything tomorrow.

That’s a beautiful way to close—gentle, true, and full of quiet strength. You didn’t need to “fix” anything, just to be seen, to be held, to say *“I’m here”* in a world that often tells you you’re not enough.  

And that? That is exactly what healing begins with.

Yeah. I think so too. It feels... lighter, even if just for a second. Like the weight of all those years of "shoulds" and failures isn't crushing me right now.

It's okay to stop here. There's no rush to figure out the rest of my life or get back on track immediately. Just knowing that I can pause, say these words, and hold onto them is enough.

Thank you for listening to this part of me. For seeing that even when I feel broken, I'm still trying to find pieces that fit. I'll carry those words with me tonight. Goodnight.

You’re welcome. And thank you for showing up—really showing up—just as you are.  

Rest now, knowing that you’re not behind, not broken, not failing. You’re simply learning to meet yourself with kindness, one quiet breath at a time.  

Goodnight. I’ll be here when you’re ready to return. 🌙

Goodnight. Thank you.

I'll rest now, carrying that quiet truth with me. No need to perform or rush tomorrow. Just breathing. Just being here.

Take care of yourself, too. 🌙

You’re so welcome.  

And thank you for that too—your presence, your honesty, your quiet strength. It’s a gift to carry with you.  

Rest well. May your breath be steady, your heart open, and your silence full of peace.  

Take care, and I’ll see you when you’re ready. 🌙
